title: Full, conscious, active (Sacrosanctum Concilium 14)
hookLine: the council's hope for how everyone takes part
tomorrow: who is the Church's light really for?

cards: At a concert there's the crowd that sings every word, and the crowd that films it. Same song, same room, two different nights. At Mass the priest leads the prayers, the choir sings, a reader takes the ambo.
So what's left for the person halfway back in the pew, holding a coat? In paragraph fourteen of its document on the liturgy, the council answers with three words, and they ask a lot.

teach.b: First, the hope. The council says Mother Church earnestly desires that all the faithful be led to full, conscious and active participation in the liturgy. Full: the whole person, not a corner of the attention.
Conscious: knowing what's happening and meaning it. Active: actually taking part. The reason is baptism.

The council quotes First Peter: "a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation, a purchased people." Taking part is the baptized people's right and their duty. Second, what active looks like.

A later paragraph, number thirty, lists acclamations, responses, psalms and songs, gestures and postures, and then a surprise: at the proper times, a reverent silence. Active includes being still on purpose.
Third, a neighbor who prizes the same thing, in its own words. In a synagogue, when the Kaddish is said, the congregation answers together in Aramaic: amen, may his great name be blessed.
The Talmud, in the tractate Shabbat, teaches that whoever answers that amen with all their strength has a harsh decree against them torn up.
Both ask the people in the seats for more than being there: their whole voice.

Fourth, one honest difference. In the synagogue, that answer centers on praising God's name. At Mass, the responses gather around the altar and the Eucharist, which Catholics believe is Christ's body.
Neither is a copy of the other.

how: At Mass, Catholics in the pews sing, say the responses and acclamations, stand, sit and kneel together, and keep moments of silence; in a synagogue, the congregation answers the Kaddish together.

o: a church packed to the doors on Easter
a stomach after a parish potluck supper
the whole person taking part, not one corner

games.q: three words, and a neighbor's amen — tap the pairs.
p: amen, may his great name be blessed

s: at Mass, the priest takes part and the people watch
the council hopes for the full, conscious, active participation of all the faithful.
the council counts reverent silence as taking part
paragraph thirty lists it, at the proper times.
in Jewish prayer the congregation's amen is a small thing
the Talmud prizes the Kaddish amen answered with all one's strength.

games.q: on a retreat, the group keeps a long silence after the Gospel. a new friend whispers: so we just sit here doing nothing? what does the council say?
o: the silence is taking part; it's on the council's list.
it's a break until the real participation starts again.
silence is only for the priest, to get ready for what's next.
games.why: Sacrosanctum Concilium 30 lists a reverent silence, at the proper times, among the ways the people take part.

practice: Sit as you might in a pew, feet down, hands at rest. Say one response aloud, the way a congregation does, Amen or Thanks be to God, and mean every syllable. Then keep a reverent silence, the kind the council counts as taking part.

wordCard.voice: Full. The first of the council's three words for how everyone takes part in the liturgy: the whole person, present. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin in Sacrosanctum Concilium 14 for active participation.

carryVoice: Your line: full and active. On the council's list, even the silence counts. That's today.

sources.work: Second Vatican Council, Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy
